walkthroughs.body_html: A. J. Ayer's Language, Truth and Logic (1936) introduced British readers to the Vienna Circle's verificationism. A genuine factual claim must be at least in principle verifiable by sense experience. 'God exists' is, on Ayer's view, neither true nor false but literally nonsense, alongside ethical and aesthetic claims.

The strong verification principle (conclusive verifiability) excludes universal statements like 'all swans are white' and so was abandoned. Ayer's weak version asks only that some possible observation count toward the truth of a statement. Critics noted that the principle itself is neither analytic nor empirically verifiable, and so seems self-refuting.

In The Existence of God (1964), John Hick told a parable: two travellers walk a road, one believing it leads to a Celestial City, the other denying it. They cannot settle the issue en route, but on arrival the question is decided. Religious statements are, Hick argues, in principle verifiable after death and so meaningful on a weak verification criterion.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.

If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
